opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the pain points have shifted quite a bit over the last couple of years. Early on, the biggest question was simply "can the model do this at all?" Today, for most enterprise use cases, the models are capable enough. The pain is really in everything around the model.

The first one is cost and efficiency. A lot of companies build a prototype on a top-tier API, it works beautifully in a demo, and then they do the math on running it at production scale with millions of requests a day, and the numbers just don't work. So they have to figure out how to optimize inference, use smaller or fine-tuned models, or mix and match. That's an engineering problem many teams aren't set up to handle.

The second is reliability and quality in production. In a demo you can cherry-pick. In production you need consistent latency, high availability, and outputs you can trust. Evaluation is surprisingly hard: how do you know a new model version or a prompt change actually made things better and didn't break some edge case? Most companies don't yet have a mature eval practice the way they have unit tests for traditional software.

The third is data and customization. The real value for a business comes from combining the model with its own proprietary data and workflows. But that data is often messy, siloed, and sensitive, so there are real concerns about privacy, compliance, and where the data goes. Many customers want to run models in their own environment or have strong guarantees about data handling.

And finally, there's the infrastructure and talent gap. Running GPUs efficiently, managing deployments, and keeping up with a field where a new state-of-the-art model comes out every few weeks is a lot. Most businesses don't want to become AI infrastructure companies. They want to focus on their product. So a big part of what we try to do is abstract that complexity away, giving them a simple, efficient, reliable platform so they can focus on the application layer where their real differentiation lies.

So in short: the model is no longer the bottleneck. Cost, reliability, data integration, and operational complexity are where customers really struggle.

r001.rationale: The response says model capability is no longer the main issue and identifies the challenge as applying models in business production through cost, reliability, proprietary data, and operational complexity.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the biggest pain point isn't really the models themselves anymore. A couple of years ago, the question was "can the model do this at all?" Today, for most business use cases, the answer is yes, or close enough. The real pain shows up the moment you try to move from a demo to something that actually runs in production.

The first thing people hit is cost and latency. It's very easy to build a prototype on a frontier model and get excited. Then you look at the bill at scale, or you realize a customer-facing feature can't wait eight seconds for a response. So now you're thinking about smaller models, quantization, batching, caching, which hardware you're on, whether you're using GPUs efficiently. That's infrastructure work, and most companies don't have a team that has done it before.

The second one is choice overload. There are open models, closed models, new ones every few weeks. Customers ask me, "Which one should I use?" and the honest answer is "it depends on your workload," which is not what they want to hear. They need a way to evaluate on their own data, swap models without rewriting everything, and not get locked into one vendor. Building that evaluation and abstraction layer is painful if you do it from scratch.

Third, and this is underrated, is data and integration. The model is maybe twenty percent of the system. The other eighty percent is getting your documents cleaned up, connecting to your internal tools, handling permissions, logging, monitoring when outputs drift. Companies underestimate how much glue there is.

And finally, there's an organizational piece. Someone has to own this. Is it the data team, the platform team, the product team? When nobody owns the operational side, projects stall right after the proof of concept.

So my framing is that AI adoption is turning from a research problem into an infrastructure and engineering problem. That's actually good news. Engineering problems are solvable, and that's where a lot of the real value is going to get created over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response says models can handle most use cases, then identifies the challenge as moving from demos to production in a business—covering cost, integration, operations, and ownership.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest pain point is the gap between getting a model to do something impressive in a demo and making it useful in a real business. A demo can work with a few carefully chosen examples. In production, you need it to work reliably with your own data, fit into existing workflows, and deliver value at a reasonable cost.

That starts with figuring out what problem you actually want to solve. Do you want to help a support agent find answers faster, or do you want to automate the entire customer interaction? Those are very different requirements. If you don’t define the task clearly, it’s hard to choose a model or even measure whether it’s working.

Then there’s the engineering around the model: connecting to internal data, managing access, evaluating quality, and handling latency and cost as usage grows. The model is one component of that system. For many businesses, the challenge is putting those pieces together without needing a large team of AI specialists.

r001.rationale: It contrasts an impressive model demo with making a model useful in a real business, then describes defining business tasks and integrating the model into workflows and systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest pain point is the gap between getting a model to do something interesting in a demo and making it useful in a real business. A demo can work with a few examples. In production, you need it to work reliably across many different situations, with acceptable cost and latency.

A lot of that work is around the model: connecting it to your company’s data, integrating it into existing workflows, and figuring out how to evaluate whether the answers are good enough. If the model makes a mistake, how do you catch it? When should a person review the result?

And then there’s the business question: What problem are you actually solving? I think customers make the most progress when they start with a specific task where they can measure the benefit, and then choose the model and infrastructure that fit that task.

r001.rationale: It contrasts getting a model to do something interesting in a demo with making it useful in a real business, then describes applying it to company data, workflows, and measurable tasks.
